hints: Think about why $A_r$ is rarely a whole number, it averages over all the isotopes present weighted by their abundances.
Recall what standard all relative masses are compared against, the atom chosen to have a mass of exactly 12.
walkthrough:
Spot the two ideas every $A_r$ definition needs**
You need an average part and a comparison part. The average part is needed because most elements are a mixture of isotopes, so you take the weighted average mass of all the atoms present. The comparison part is needed because $A_r$ has no units, it is relative.

Lock in the standard**
Cambridge always uses the same standard: a $^{12}\text{C}$ atom is defined as exactly 12. So you compare to $1/12$ of the mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$. Put both ideas together and you have the full two mark definition.
Final answer: The average weighted mass of an atom of an element compared to $1/12$ of the mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$.

hints: Start by finding the missing percentage, the three abundances must add to 100%.
Set up the weighted average equation $A_r = \Sigma(\text{isotopic mass} \times \%)/100$ with the unknown mass as $x$ and solve.
walkthrough:
Find the missing abundance**
You are told there are three isotopes but only two percentages. Percentages must total 100, so:
$$100 - 91.9 - 6.0 = 2.1\%$$
That $2.1\%$ belongs to the unknown isotope.

Write the $A_r$ equation and solve**
$A_r$ is the weighted average:
$$A_r = \frac{\Sigma(\text{mass} \times \%)}{100}$$
Substitute $A_r = 55.8$ and let the unknown mass be $x$:
$$55.8 = \frac{(53.9 \times 6.0) + (55.9 \times 91.9) + (x \times 2.1)}{100}$$
$$5580 = 323.4 + 5137.21 + 2.1x$$
$$2.1x = 119.39$$
$$x = 56.9 \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

Final answer: Abundance of third isotope $= 100 - 91.9 - 6.0 = 2.1\%$
$$55.8 = \frac{(53.9 \times 6.0) + (55.9 \times 91.9) + (x \times 2.1)}{100}$$
relative isotopic mass $= 56.9$

hints: Write the configuration of Fe first ($Z = 26$), then remember that transition metals lose $4s$ electrons before $3d$ electrons to form ions.
walkthrough:
Get to $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ correctly**
Fe is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^6 4s^2$. When it forms $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ it loses the two $4s$ electrons first, leaving $3d^6$. Now count pairs in the $3d$ sub-shell. There are five $3d$ orbitals. Fill singly first, then pair: six electrons gives four unpaired electrons plus one paired set. So there is 1 pair.

hints: List the sub-shells present in shell $n = 2$ and pick which type ($s$ or $p$) is lower in energy.
walkthrough:
Identify the lowest orbital in shell 2**
Shell $n = 2$ contains $2s$ and $2p$ sub-shells. The $s$ sub-shell is always lower in energy than $p$ in the same shell, so the lowest energy orbital is $2s$. All $s$ orbitals are spherical, so simply draw a circle to represent the boundary surface.
Final answer: A circle (spherical $2s$ orbital) centred on the nucleus.

hints: Use the atomic number of Fe ($Z = 26$) to find protons, then subtract the $3+$ charge to get electrons in the ion.
Use mass number minus atomic number to get neutrons, the charge does not affect neutron count.
walkthrough:
Count electrons in $^{56}\text{Fe}^{3+}$**
Fe has atomic number 26, so a neutral Fe atom has 26 protons and 26 electrons. The $3+$ charge means three electrons have been lost:
$$26 - 3 = 23 \text{ electrons}$$

Count neutrons**
Neutrons $=$ mass number $-$ atomic number:
$$56 - 26 = 30 \text{ neutrons}$$
So the completed table is electrons 23 and neutrons 30. Protons stay at 26, the charge only changes electrons.

Final answer: electrons $= 23$; particle with 30 present is neutrons
neutrons $= 56 - 26 = 30$

hints: Compare the electron count in Fe ($26$ electrons) with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($23$ electrons) and think about which shell is lost.
Think about what happens to the pull of the same $26$ protons on fewer electrons with less shielding.
walkthrough:
Decide smaller or larger**
Fe is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^6 4s^2$. To make $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ it loses both $4s$ electrons and one $3d$ electron. The whole $n = 4$ outer shell is removed, so the outermost electrons are now in $n = 3$, much closer to the nucleus. The ion must be smaller.

Explain the stronger pull**
The nuclear charge is still $26$ protons, but there are now only $23$ electrons with less electron-electron repulsion and less shielding. The same nucleus pulls more strongly on fewer shells, drawing them in further. That is why the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ionic radius is much smaller than the $1.26 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$ atomic radius.

Final answer: Radius decreases / smaller.
Loss of the outer / $4s$ shell of electrons so the remaining electrons experience greater nuclear attraction.
